summary: Specifies the QCP file format, which many implementations already used to store QCELP 13K speech and also EVRC and SMV vocoder data. RFC 2658 covered the streaming format but not storage. This document also updates the audio/qcelp media type and registers audio/evrc-qcp and audio/smv-qcp.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3625 describes the QCP file, the container that programs used to store speech compressed by the QCELP, EVRC or SMV cellular codecs. The file is a sequence of chunks: one describing the codec, one describing how the packets vary in size, and the data chunk holding the speech frames themselves. The document also registers the media types that name this format.

subtitle: The container file used to store QCELP, EVRC and SMV speech frames on disk

tldr.problem: Speech codecs for cellular networks had a well known streaming format but no agreed way to store their frames in a file, so every program that saved a recording wrote its own container.
tldr.mechanism: The document specifies the QCP file format with an ABNF grammar: a RIFF-style header followed by chunks that describe the codec, the packet sizes, the time offsets and the speech data itself. It also updates the audio/qcelp media registration to name this format for storage.
tldr.outcome: The format was already in wide use in mail clients, multimedia software and handsets when it was written down, and the document adds the audio/evrc-qcp and audio/smv-qcp media types and marks audio/vnd.qcelp as deprecated.

facts.label: Magic bytes
facts.value: RIFF at offset 0 and QLCM at offset 8

facts.label: QCP format versions
facts.value: 1.0 for QCELP-13K and EVRC, 2.0 for SMV

today: RFC 3625 is an Informational memo from 2003, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The format was already in wide use when it was documented, so the document registers media types for it and updates two earlier registrations rather than defining a new protocol.

sections.title: Why a File Format for Speech
sections.content:
The document specifies the QCP format for storage of QCELP 13K, EVRC and SMV vocoder frames in files which may reside on network elements such as media servers and Multimedia Messaging System centers and on third-generation cellular handsets, or be transmitted by email or other mechanisms. Vocoder frames read from a QCP file may be streamed using protocols and formats outside the scope of the document, delivered to an EVRC, SMV or QCELP 13K decoder, or otherwise processed.

The QCP format supports QCELP 13K as well as EVRC and SMV data, and it is different from the EVRC and SMV storage format specified in the RTP payload format document for those two codecs.

The reason for writing the document is that the format was already in use. Many implementations had been using the QCP file format, named for its file extension, for exchanging QCELP 13K data as well as EVRC and SMV data, for example in mail user agents, quicktime players and cdma2000 handsets. The document therefore specifies the format, updates the audio/qcelp media registration to point at this specification for storage, and registers the audio/evrc-qcp and audio/smv-qcp media types for EVRC and SMV data stored in this way.
sections.plainLanguage: The cellular speech codecs could be streamed in a standard way, but there was no standard way to save them. This document writes down the container that programs were already using, so that files could be exchanged between them.

sections.title: The Chunk Layout of a QCP File
sections.content:
The whole file is described by one grammar rule: a qcp file is a RIFF container of type QLCM, followed by a format chunk, a variable rate chunk, and then optionally a label chunk, an offset chunk, the data chunk, and optionally a configuration chunk and a text chunk.

The size fields follow the RIFF convention. The riff-size field is the total size of the file in bytes, excluding the size of the RIFF and riff-size fields themselves. Each chunk-size field is the total size of the chunk it describes, excluding the size of the chunk-size field and any elements before it in the rule, as well as the pad element if one is present. A pad byte of value zero is present only when the number of bytes in the chunk would otherwise be odd, and its size is not counted in any chunk-size field.

The chunks carry specific information. The format chunk holds the version of the QCP file format and the codec information. The variable rate chunk holds a flag saying whether the packets have a fixed size and the total number of packets in the data chunk. The label chunk holds 48 octets for general application use. The offset chunk holds a step size in increments of 100 milliseconds and the offsets of packets in time order, so that a player can find the packet for a given moment. The data chunk holds the packets themselves, with as many packets as the size-in-packets field elsewhere in the file says. The configuration chunk holds a bitmapped word for application use, and the text chunk holds a zero-terminated string of application information.
sections.plainLanguage: The file is a sequence of labelled blocks, each with a size field, in the same style as the audio files a computer plays. One block describes the codec, one says how big the packets are and how many there are, one gives the timing of each packet, and the data block holds the speech itself.

sections.title: Codec Information and Packet Sizes
sections.content:
The format chunk carries the codec information: a codec identifier, a codec version, a codec name of up to 80 octets, the average data rate, the size of the largest possible packet, the number of samples encoded in every packet, the sampling rate, the number of bits per sample, and a variable-rate field followed by five reserved 32-bit values that should be set to zero for now, with readers told to allow non-zero values when reading files.

The codec identifier is a unique value for the codec used to encode the packets, and the elements match the structure of a GUID in other specifications, with the first three stored in little-endian octet order. Four codec identifiers are defined: two for QCELP-13K, one for EVRC and one for SMV. The codec version is 1 or 2 for QCELP-13K and 1 for EVRC and SMV. The sampling rate is the number of speech samples per second, typically 8000, and the sample size is the number of bits per speech sample, typically 16.

The variable rate flag decides how a packet's size is found. If it is zero, the packets in the data chunk are fixed at the size given by the packet-size field. If it is greater than zero but less than %xFFFF0000, the packets are variable rate and the rate octet at the start of each packet determines its size, using the rate map table. Values of %xFFFF0001 and higher are reserved for future versions of the format. The rate map table holds eight entries, each mapping a possible rate octet to the size of the rest of a packet with that rate octet, and unused entries should be filled with zeroes.

The grammar also notes that a codec rate octet is always present in a packet, even in a fixed-size file, where the first octet of the packet is still considered the rate for the packet even though it is not part of the syntax.
sections.plainLanguage: The format block says which codec made the speech, what version, how fast it samples the voice, and how big each packet is. When the packets vary in size, a small table says how to work out the size of a packet from the rate byte at its start.

sections.title: Media Type Registrations
sections.content:
The IANA has updated the audio/qcelp and audio/vnd.qcelp registrations and has added the audio/evrc-qcp and audio/smv-qcp registrations.

The audio/qcelp registration has been updated to indicate that this specification is to be used for storage. The audio/vnd.qcelp registration has been updated to indicate that use of that media type is deprecated, and to note that audio/qcelp should be used instead.

The two new registrations, audio/evrc-qcp and audio/smv-qcp, have no required or optional parameters. The storage format may be used with any transport mechanism. The magic number is the first four octets RIFF, with the octets 9 to 12 holding QLCM; the octets 5 to 8 hold the riff-size field, which is the size of the file minus the RIFF header, so it is not fixed and cannot be part of the magic number. The file extensions are qcp and QCP, there is no Macintosh file type code and no object identifier. The intended usage is COMMON, because the format is already in wide use in Internet email user agents, multimedia authoring and playing software, and cdma2000 handsets. The change controller is the IETF.
sections.plainLanguage: The document sorts out the labels that name this format. The existing qcelp label now points at the storage format, the older vnd.qcelp label is marked as not to be used, and two new labels are registered for the EVRC and SMV versions.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document specifies a file format only, not a streaming protocol payload format and not a transfer method. As such it introduces no security risks beyond those associated with any audio codec or media file format, for example a denial of service by transmitting a file larger than the receiver can handle. The document notes that those concerns should be understood before the format is used.
sections.plainLanguage: Because this is only a container for speech frames, it adds no security risk of its own. The usual risks of media files apply, such as sending a file that is too big for the receiver.

viz.caption: The top-level grammar of a QCP file, copied from the RFC

data.title: qcp-file
data.code:
qcp-file  = riff-qlcm fmt vrat [labl] [offs] data [cnfg] [text]

riff-qlcm = RIFF riff-size QLCM
fmt       = FMT chunk-size major minor codec-info
vrat      = VRAT chunk-size var-rate-flag size-in-packets
labl      = LABL chunk-size label
offs      = OFFS chunk-size step-size num-offsets *offset
data      = DATA chunk-size *packet [pad]
cnfg      = CNFG chunk-size config
text      = TEXT chunk-size string [pad]

items.title: RIFF and QLCM
items.text: The first four octets are RIFF and octets 9 to 12 are QLCM, with the file size between them.

items.title: FMT
items.text: The version of the QCP format and the codec information: identifier, version, name, rates and packet sizes.

items.title: VRAT
items.text: A flag saying whether packets are fixed size, and the total number of packets in the data chunk.

items.title: LABL
items.text: 48 octets kept for general application use.

items.title: OFFS
items.text: A step size in 100ms increments and the offset of each packet in time order.

items.title: DATA
items.text: The packets themselves, as many as the size-in-packets field says.

items.title: CNFG and TEXT
items.text: A bitmapped configuration word and a zero-terminated string, both for application use.
